name: Self-deception
statement: People are said to hide an unwelcome belief from themselves, holding the flattering version while some part of them registers the true one.
meaning: Sackeim and Gur set four conditions for calling something self-deception. The person holds two contradictory beliefs, holds them at the same time, is unaware of one of them, and that unawareness is motivated. All four have to hold. The last two are what separate the claim from ordinary error and from ordinary flattery. Someone who says a kind thing about himself and believes it is not deceiving himself, he is simply wrong, or right. The interesting case is someone who reports the flattering answer while another part of him holds the true one, and that is the case laboratory work has struggled to catch. Published demonstrations mostly show a person producing a favourable judgement in conditions where a plainer motive would produce the same judgement. Establishing the second, hidden belief is the difficult half, and it is the half the paradigms argue about.

origin.who: Ruben C. Gur and Harold A. Sackeim
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper is titled "Self-deception: A concept in search of a phenomenon". The criteria had been set out the year before, in a chapter called "Self-deception, self-confrontation, and consciousness" in volume 2 of Consciousness and Self-Regulation. The voice task itself is older: Greenwald traces it to Wolff in 1932. The word is far older than any of this, and 1979 is the date of the first sustained attempt to make it a laboratory finding.

evidence: Gur and Sackeim's paradigm records a person's voice, plays back a mixed series of samples, and asks after each one whether the voice is theirs. Skin conductance is recorded throughout. Self-deception is scored when the skin response marks an own-voice trial that the person calls not mine. The description here is Greenwald's, because the 1979 paper could not be opened. Quattrone and Tversky ran a different design on 38 Stanford undergraduates, who held a forearm in circulating cold water before and after a minute on an exercise bicycle. Half were told a strong heart shows up as more cold tolerance after exercise, half that it shows up as less. Mean immersion fell from 44.74 to 37.11 seconds in the decrease condition and rose from 34.21 to 46.05 seconds in the increase condition, F(1, 36) = 30.64, p < .001. Only 9 of the 38 said they had tried to alter their time. Two of those nine inferred the healthy heart type, against 20 of the 29 who denied trying, p < .05, and the two groups had shifted by similar amounts. Those figures come from the June 1983 Office of Naval Research technical report, since the 1984 journal version could not be opened. Its publisher answers a bot challenge rather than asking for money. Chance, Norton, Gino and Ariely ran four experiments on 421 people, half of whom took a test with the answer key printed at the foot of the page. A separate group of 36, who only imagined taking such a test, is not one of the four. In their second experiment the answer group scored 8.97 out of 10 against the control group's 6.29, then predicted 7.73 on a second test with no key, against 6.32, t(129) = 4.04, p < .001. Both groups then scored about 5. Schwardmann and van der Weele ran two experiments on 688 people who first sat an intelligence test. Half were told they could earn 15 euros by convincing an employer, face to face, that they had done well. Their privately elicited confidence, taken before any meeting, was higher than the control group's, pooled d = 0.31, p < .001. The first experiment on its own reached only P = 0.049.

examples.tag: The swelling that is nothing to worry about
examples.text: A woman decides a swelling is nothing, books no appointment, and reads about it late at night while choosing looser clothes. Her conduct follows the possibility she says she has ruled out, and the claim needs both positions held at once rather than one of them simply being wrong.

examples.tag: The shop that is only having a slow month
examples.text: A shopkeeper insists trade is quiet for the season, stops opening the bank letters and starts paying suppliers late. The behaviour tracks a shortfall he denies, and the denial has to be motivated rather than careless for the label to apply.

examples.tag: The marriage going through a patch
examples.text: A man tells his friends nothing is wrong at home and has already worked out which of them he could stay with. The account he gives and the plans he makes rest on different beliefs, and the one he does not report is the one his planning follows.

replication.headline: The inflated prediction after cheating repeats in an independent sample. The step from that to a hidden second belief does not survive its critics.
replication.detail: Liu and colleagues ran the Chance design on 47 Chinese students, swapping general knowledge for a dot-estimation task. The answer group predicted 33.81 on a 50-item second test against the control group's 27.00, F(1, 45) = 7.11, p < .05, while actual second-test scores were 19.90 and 20.65, F(1, 45) = 0.64. Their second experiment, on 93 students, reproduced that gap where no feedback was given and removed it where participants were told their first score was low. Schwardmann and van der Weele's follow-up on 400 people repeated their own first result, t(398) = 2.75, P = 0.0063, d = 0.32, which matters because dropping one outlier from their first experiment of 288 takes it below the 5% threshold, as they report themselves. The older paradigms have gone the other way. Douglas and Gibbins produced a comparable physiological pattern from people trying to identify the voice of a familiar acquaintance rather than their own, which removes the motive the account needs. Sackeim and Gur replied in 1985 that no evidence had been given that the errors were not self-deception, and Gibbins and Douglas answered in the same issue. Zhang and Rand then attacked the persuasion strand with two preregistered experiments of 1,609 and 2,399 people. Assigning people to summarise arguments rather than to persuade with them produced the same belief shift, and a prior summary task cut the later shift about fivefold, which points at exposure rather than at a motive to persuade. No direct replication of Quattrone and Tversky's cold-water experiment was located.

study.cite: Liu, J., Zhang, W., Zhan, Y., Song, L., Guan, P., Kang, D., Jian, J., Cai, R., & Li, M. (2019). The effect of negative feedback on positive beliefs in self-deception. Frontiers in Psychology, 10, 702.

limits: The hard part is unproved. Each design shows a person giving a flattering answer, and none of them isolates a second, unwelcome belief held at the same moment. Greenwald offers a reading of the voice task that needs no hidden belief: the skin response can be driven by acoustic features resembling one's own voice, at a stage before any identification, the way an envelope can be taken for junk mail without being opened. Quattrone and Tversky raise their own alternative, a motivational placebo effect in which wanting the shift produces a real change in tolerance rather than a deliberate one. They also note that denial is not all or none. Their journal version could not be obtained, so the figures on this page come from the technical report and may differ from print. Gur and Sackeim's own numbers could not be read off their paper and are left out. Two authors of the cheating study have had other work retracted, including a 2012 PNAS paper on dishonesty co-authored by Gino and Ariely that Crossref lists as retracted, and that entry 379 covers; the 2011 self-deception paper carries no retraction notice in Crossref or PubMed. Paulhus's Self-Deceptive Enhancement scale, the trait measure used in that study, was built on Sackeim and Gur's split between conscious and unconscious bias, and Paulhus and John later dropped that split as the organising axis, recasting the two factors as agentic and communal in content. They also say plainly that their method studies a gap between self-ratings and the ratings of informed observers, rather than verifying that the person is aware of the observer's view.
misreadings: The philosophical puzzle is not the finding. Whether one mind can both know and not know a thing is a question about the concept, and Greenwald's answer is that abandoning the assumption of a single unified knower dissolves it. Kurzban's commentary on von Hippel and Trivers is titled for the same move, and his abstract says a modular view of the mind finesses the problem of a self to be deceived. The argument beneath the title is narrower. He accepts the arms-race account where an audience is present, and objects only to calling a plain bias self-deception when no outside party is being fooled. Second, von Hippel and Trivers' proposal is often reported as settled. Their 2011 target article argues that self-deception evolved because it hides the cues that give a liar away, and the journal ran it with open commentary. Dunning's reply says the claim carries too many implications to be promoted by indirect argument and belongs in a laboratory, and offers the alternative that better deceivers are people who do not care about the truth. Third, a high score on a self-deception questionnaire is not evidence that anyone deceived themselves. It is a report of positive self-regard, and Paulhus and Holden group those scales under self-enhancement. Fourth, the cold-water result is retold as people fooling themselves about their hearts. What was measured is a shift in immersion time and a denial of intent on an anonymous questionnaire, and Quattrone and Tversky's own claim was the narrower one, that the diagnosis was accepted mainly by the people who denied trying.

The paradigm is described here from Greenwald's 1997 chapter.
